text.p: If I were computer (and thank God I'm not) I'd say it was time to lay real low.

For too long now, computers have been befuddling us, crashing on us, acting up and generally getting the last laugh. I mean who but a computer would utter a line like this when something goes wrong: "This programme has performed an illegal operation and will be shut down." Or how about everybody's favourite computer line: "Fatal Error."
Well, as the saying goes, we're not going to take it anymore.
While not condoning violence, I offer up as evidence a July 12, 1997 headline from the Seattle-Post Intelligencer: "Lone gunman shoots computer in frustration."

"A 43-year-old Issaquah man," began the front page article, "lodging an existential protest against modern technology, hauled out a pistol late Wednesday night and pumped five rounds into his personal computer."
"...aside from the computer no one was injured."

The man became infuriated when the computer didn't work and his remedy was to put himself out of misery by shooting the computer. The shooter, after taking out the hard drive and other vital electronic organs, was taken to a nearby hospital for "careful" supervision. Let's just hope the hospital was not decked out with a lot of computerized monitoring devices which would have only set back his recuperation time.
The newspaper reporter found that this was the second computer gunned down in the area in the past two years, although local experts did not think it was that common of a crime.

Many of you, of course, might think this is just an isolated incident, but there are a growing number of tales out there of people getting really, really frustrated with those ominous computers sitting on their desks.

We have all heard the tales of people slamming on computer screens and on their computer keyboards. We have witnessed people toss around their mouse like it really was some kind of rodent they wanted to kill. People have blamed heart attacks, fits of rage and even moments of insanity on their computers. Many think their machines act more like HAL, the computer of "2001: A Space Odyssey" than some simple office productivity tool.

Take, for example, Nicholas Negroponte, who has been described as one of the Ayatollahs of the Internet. He's been a professor, authored books and writes from the near holy space on the back page of Wired Magazine. You might think he would be the last guy on earth to get frustrated with computers.

"I am amazed that so many people use Windows 95 without complaint. I guess there is a grin and-bear-it attitude because THERE IS NOTHING ELSE. Yes, I am yelling." Negroponte, well, yelled, in a recent column.

He was describing his efforts to update his systems with the latest programmes and was dumbfounded about how complicated and slow everthing was. (If you happened to be a member of some computer hugging conservation society you might consider draping yourself over his machines because I don't think they are long with this life).

"Have you looked at the size and complexity of Microsoft Word recently? Outrageous. And each successive version has gotten worse. It's to the point where most programmes are almost unusable and run slower than what I used a decade ago. What is wrong with you Redmond folk?" Negroponte continued.

We can either expect a lot more violent outbursts like this if things don't get better soon. It's either that or we can adopt a more Zen like attitude, which a computer expert named Michael Goodwin suggested as his way of coping in the Post-Intelligencer article.
"You learn patience, or you learn to drink," Goodwin said.
